lessons.title: Forms and Input
lessons.content: Forms collect user data: <form> wraps inputs. Types: text, password, email, number, checkbox, radio, date, file. <textarea> for multi-line. <select>/<option> for dropdowns. <button type='submit'> submits. <label> describes inputs (accessibility). Required attribute prevents empty submission. Placeholder shows hint text. Form action attribute specifies where data is sent.

keyTerms.required: Attribute preventing form submission if empty

quiz.question: Which hides typed characters?
quiz.explanation: password shows dots/asterisks.

quiz.question: <label> does:
quiz.explanation: Labels describe inputs — clicking label focuses the input.

quiz.question: Dropdown menu tag:
quiz.explanation: select with option children creates dropdowns.

quiz.question: required attribute:

quiz.question: type='email' helps by:
quiz.explanation: Browsers check for valid email format (must contain @) before submitting.

lessons.title: Tables and Multimedia
lessons.content: Tables display data in rows and columns. <table> wraps everything, <tr> creates rows, <th> for header cells (bold, centered), <td> for data cells. <thead>, <tbody>, <tfoot> organize table sections. colspan and rowspan merge cells. For multimedia: <video> embeds video with controls attribute, <audio> embeds sound. <iframe> embeds external content (YouTube, maps). <canvas> creates graphics with JavaScript. Always provide alternative content for multimedia (subtitles for video, alt text for images).

keyTerms.table: HTML element for displaying data in rows and columns
keyTerms.th: Table header cell — bold and centered by default
keyTerms.iframe: Inline frame — embeds external content like videos or maps

quiz.question: <th> creates:
quiz.explanation: th = table header, displayed bold and centered. td = regular data.

quiz.question: To merge two columns in a table:
quiz.explanation: colspan merges cells horizontally across columns.

quiz.question: The controls attribute on <video>:
quiz.explanation: controls adds the standard video player interface for the user.

quiz.question: To embed a YouTube video:
options: Use <iframe> with the YouTube embed URL
quiz.explanation: YouTube provides iframe embed codes for embedding videos in web pages.

quiz.question: Why provide subtitles for videos?
options: Accessibility — for deaf/hard-of-hearing users and non-native speakers
quiz.explanation: Subtitles/captions ensure video content is accessible to all users.

lessons.title: HTML5 Semantic Structure
lessons.content: HTML5 introduced semantic elements that describe their content's purpose, replacing generic <div> containers. <header> contains introductory content or navigation. <nav> wraps main navigation links. <main> contains the primary page content (one per page). <article> is self-contained content (blog post, news story). <section> groups related content within a page. <aside> is secondary content (sidebar, related links). <footer> contains closing content (copyright, contact). Using semantic HTML improves: accessibility (screen readers understand structure), SEO (search engines understand content), and code readability. Always use the most specific semantic tag available.

keyTerms.semantic HTML: Tags that describe their content's purpose (header, nav, main, article)
keyTerms.article: Self-contained content that makes sense independently
keyTerms.section: A thematic grouping of content within a page
keyTerms.aside: Content tangentially related to the main content (sidebars)

quiz.question: How many <main> elements should a page have?
options: Two — one for mobile, one for desktop
quiz.explanation: A page should have exactly one <main> containing the primary content.

quiz.question: <article> is best for:
options: Self-contained content like a blog post or news story
quiz.explanation: article wraps content that makes sense on its own — could be syndicated independently.

quiz.question: Why use semantic HTML over <div> everywhere?
quiz.explanation: Semantic tags tell browsers, search engines, and screen readers what content means.

quiz.question: <aside> is typically used for:
quiz.explanation: Aside contains content related to but not essential for the main content.

quiz.question: <nav> should contain:
options: Major navigation links for the site
quiz.explanation: nav wraps the main navigation — not every link on the page needs to be in nav.

lessons.title: Introduction to CSS
lessons.content: CSS controls how HTML looks — colors, fonts, spacing, layout. Rules have selector and declarations: h1 { color: blue; font-size: 24px; }. Three ways: inline (style attribute), internal (<style> in head), external (.css file — best). Colors: named (red), hex (#FF0000), RGB (rgb(255,0,0)), HSL. Cascade: later styles override earlier; more specific selectors win. Selectors: element (p), class (.myclass), ID (#myid), descendant (div p).

keyTerms.specificity: How specific a selector is — more specific wins

quiz.question: CSS stands for:
quiz.explanation: CSS = Cascading Style Sheets.

quiz.question: Best way to add CSS:
quiz.explanation: External CSS separates styling and is reusable.

quiz.question: #FF0000 is:
quiz.explanation: FF red, 00 green, 00 blue = pure red.

quiz.question: Which selector is most specific?
quiz.explanation: ID selectors (#) are more specific than classes (.) which are more specific than elements.

quiz.question: To style all elements with class 'highlight':
quiz.explanation: Period (.) selects by class name.

lessons.title: Box Model and Layout
lessons.content: Every element is a box: content + padding + border + margin. Control size: width, height. Display: block (full width: div, p, h1), inline (content width: span, a), inline-block, none (hidden). Flexbox: display: flex — arrange items in rows/columns. Grid: display: grid — 2D layouts. Box-sizing: border-box includes padding and border in width calculation.
examples: div { padding: 20px; margin: 10px; border: 1px solid black; }
.container { display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center; }

keyTerms.flexbox: Flexible layout in rows or columns

quiz.question: Between content and border:
quiz.explanation: Padding sits between content and border.

quiz.question: display: flex makes:

quiz.explanation: Flex enables flexible child arrangement.

quiz.question: margin: auto on block with set width:
quiz.explanation: Auto distributes remaining space equally.

quiz.question: box-sizing: border-box means:
quiz.explanation: Border-box prevents padding/border from expanding beyond set width.

quiz.question: Grid is better than flexbox for:
quiz.explanation: Grid handles 2D (rows+columns); flexbox handles 1D (row or column).

lessons.title: Responsive Design
lessons.content: Responsive design works on all screen sizes. Viewport meta: <meta name='viewport' content='width=device-width, initial-scale=1'>. Media queries: @media (max-width: 768px) { ... } targets screens ≤768px. Use relative units: %, em, rem, vw, vh instead of fixed px. Mobile-first: write mobile styles first, enhance for larger screens. Images: max-width: 100% makes them responsive. Test on real devices and browser dev tools (F12).

keyTerms.mobile-first: Write mobile styles first, enhance for larger screens

quiz.question: @media (max-width: 768px) targets:
quiz.explanation: max-width: 768px = styles apply when screen is 768px or narrower.

quiz.question: % instead of px because:
quiz.explanation: Percentages adapt to container size.

quiz.question: Mobile-first means:
options: Write mobile styles first, add desktop later
quiz.explanation: Start small, then use min-width queries to enhance.

quiz.question: rem units are relative to:
quiz.explanation: rem = root em, relative to the html element's font size.

quiz.question: To make images responsive:
quiz.explanation: max-width: 100% prevents images from exceeding their container.

lessons.title: CSS Animations and Transitions
lessons.content: Transitions smoothly animate property changes: transition: property duration timing-function delay. Example: button:hover { background: blue; transition: background 0.3s ease; } — the color change takes 0.3 seconds instead of instant. Timing functions: ease (default, slow start/end), linear (constant), ease-in (slow start), ease-out (slow end). Animations use @keyframes for complex multi-step sequences. Transform: rotate(), scale(), translate(), skew() — change element position/size without affecting layout. Hover effects (:hover) create interactive feedback. Keep animations subtle — too much movement is distracting and can cause accessibility issues.
examples: .btn { transition: all 0.3s ease; } .btn:hover { transform: scale(1.05); background: #4F46E5; }
@keyframes fadeIn { from { opacity: 0; } to { opacity: 1; } } .element { animation: fadeIn 1s ease; }

keyTerms.transition: Smooth animation between two states of a property
keyTerms.transform: Change element's position, rotation, or scale without affecting layout
keyTerms.hover: CSS pseudo-class triggered when mouse is over an element

quiz.question: transition: color 0.5s ease means:
options: Color change takes 0.5 seconds with ease timing
quiz.explanation: Transition smoothly animates the color property over 0.5 seconds.

quiz.question: @keyframes is used for:
quiz.explanation: Keyframes define what happens at each step of a complex animation.

quiz.question: transform: scale(2) does:
quiz.explanation: scale(2) makes the element twice as large in both dimensions.

quiz.question: Too many animations can:

quiz.question: ease-in timing means:
quiz.explanation: ease-in accelerates: slow start, faster finish.

lessons.title: CSS Variables and Modern Features
lessons.content: CSS Custom Properties (variables) store reusable values: :root { --primary: #4F46E5; --spacing: 16px; }. Use with var(): color: var(--primary). Change variables to update entire themes. CSS Grid advanced: grid-template-areas names regions for intuitive layout. Clamp() creates fluid typography: font-size: clamp(1rem, 2vw, 2rem) — minimum, preferred, maximum. Container queries (@container) style based on parent size, not screen size. Modern CSS reduces the need for JavaScript for many interactive features — accordions, tabs, and dark mode can all be done in pure CSS.

keyTerms.CSS variable: A custom property storing a reusable value: --name: value
keyTerms.clamp: A function setting min, preferred, and max values: clamp(min, preferred, max)
keyTerms.grid-template-areas: Named grid regions for intuitive layout planning
keyTerms.prefers-color-scheme: Media query detecting user's system dark/light mode preference

quiz.explanation: This media query checks the user's OS-level dark/light mode setting.

quiz.question: Why use CSS variables?
options: Change one value to update the whole theme consistently
quiz.explanation: Variables make themes maintainable — change --primary once, every usage updates.

lessons.title: Variables and Functions in JS
lessons.content: JavaScript makes pages interactive. Variables: let (changeable), const (fixed). Data types: strings, numbers, booleans, arrays, objects, null, undefined. Functions: function greet(name) { return 'Hello ' + name; } or arrow: const greet = (name) => 'Hello ' + name. Template literals: `Hello ${name}`. Console.log() for debugging.

quiz.question: Template literal syntax:

lessons.title: DOM Manipulation
lessons.content: DOM is the browser's HTML tree that JS can modify. Select: getElementById, querySelector, querySelectorAll. Change content: .textContent, .innerHTML. Change styles: .style.color = 'red'. Classes: .classList.add/remove/toggle. Create elements: createElement + appendChild. The DOM lets you update pages without reloading.

keyTerms.DOM: Document Object Model — browser's HTML tree
keyTerms.querySelector: Selects first element matching CSS selector

quiz.explanation: DOM = Document Object Model.

lessons.title: Events and Interactivity
lessons.content: Events are user actions: clicks, key presses, form submissions. addEventListener: button.addEventListener('click', function() { ... }). Common events: click, mouseover, keydown, submit, load, scroll. Event object: event.target (clicked element), event.key, event.preventDefault() (stop default behavior). Event delegation: attach one listener to parent, handle children via event.target — more efficient than listeners on every child.

keyTerms.event listener: Code waiting for a specific event
keyTerms.event: An action: click, keypress, submit, load
keyTerms.event delegation: One listener on parent handles events from children

quiz.question: preventDefault() commonly used with:
quiz.explanation: Forms reload the page by default — preventDefault stops this.

quiz.question: Keydown fires when:
quiz.explanation: keydown = key pressed; keyup = key released.

quiz.question: event.target gives:
options: The element that triggered the event
quiz.explanation: target is the specific element the user interacted with.

quiz.question: Event delegation is efficient because:
options: One listener handles many child elements
quiz.explanation: Instead of 100 listeners on 100 items, one on the parent catches all.

lessons.title: Fetch API and Async JavaScript
lessons.content: Modern JavaScript uses the Fetch API to make HTTP requests: fetch('url').then(response => response.json()).then(data => { ... }). Async/await is cleaner: const response = await fetch('url'); const data = await response.json(). Promises represent future results: pending → fulfilled or rejected. Error handling: try/catch with async/await. CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) may block requests to different domains. JSON is the standard data format. Local Storage stores data in the browser: localStorage.setItem('key', 'value').
examples: const res = await fetch('https://api.example.com/data'); const data = await res.json();
try { const data = await fetchData(); } catch (err) { console.error('Failed:', err); }

keyTerms.fetch: Modern API for making HTTP requests in JavaScript
keyTerms.async/await: Syntax for writing asynchronous code that looks synchronous
keyTerms.Promise: An object representing a future result — pending, fulfilled, or rejected
keyTerms.localStorage: Browser storage that persists data between sessions

quiz.question: fetch() returns:
quiz.explanation: Fetch returns a Promise that resolves with the response.

quiz.question: await can only be used inside:
quiz.explanation: await pauses execution until the Promise resolves — only works in async functions.

quiz.question: response.json() does:

quiz.explanation: .json() parses the response body as JSON.

quiz.question: CORS errors happen when:

quiz.explanation: Browsers block cross-origin requests unless the server explicitly allows them.

lessons.title: JavaScript Frameworks Overview
lessons.content: As web apps grow complex, frameworks provide structure. React (by Meta): component-based, virtual DOM, most popular, used by Facebook, Instagram, Netflix. Vue: progressive, easier learning curve, great documentation. Angular (by Google): full framework, TypeScript-based, enterprise apps. Svelte: compiles to vanilla JS, no virtual DOM, very fast. Next.js (React) and Nuxt.js (Vue) add server-side rendering for better SEO and performance. Node.js runs JavaScript on the server — enabling full-stack JS development. Choose based on project needs, team experience, and community support — there's no single 'best' framework.
examples: React component: function Button() { return <button onClick={handleClick}>Click me</button> }
Node.js server: const express = require('express'); app.get('/', (req, res) => res.send('Hello'));

keyTerms.React: Component-based JavaScript library by Meta for building user interfaces
keyTerms.Vue: Progressive JavaScript framework — easy to learn, great for small-to-medium projects
keyTerms.Node.js: JavaScript runtime that runs on the server, enabling full-stack JS development
keyTerms.component: A reusable, self-contained piece of UI with its own logic and styling

quiz.question: React is best known for:
quiz.explanation: React uses components and a virtual DOM for efficient UI updates.

quiz.question: Node.js allows:
quiz.explanation: Node.js takes JavaScript beyond the browser to server-side development.

quiz.question: Why use a framework?

quiz.question: Server-side rendering (SSR) helps with:

quiz.explanation: SSR generates HTML on the server — search engines can read it and users see content faster.

lessons.title: Project Structure
lessons.content: Good organization: root has index.html, css/ folder, js/ folder, images/ folder. Use relative paths. Naming: lowercase, hyphens. Every page needs: DOCTYPE, lang, charset, viewport meta, title, linked CSS/JS. Semantic HTML: header, nav, main, section, article, footer instead of div everywhere.

keyTerms.meta tag: Information about the page in the <head>

quiz.question: Standard homepage filename:
quiz.explanation: Servers serve index.html by default.

quiz.question: Semantic tag:

quiz.question: CSS files go in:
quiz.explanation: Organized in separate css/ folder.

quiz.question: The viewport meta tag is important for:
quiz.explanation: Without it, mobile devices render the page at desktop width and zoom out.

quiz.question: File naming convention for web:
quiz.explanation: Lowercase with hyphens avoids URL encoding issues and is universally compatible.

lessons.title: Version Control with Git
lessons.content: Git tracks code changes over time. Initialize: git init. Stage: git add. Commit: git commit -m 'message'. History: git log. GitHub stores repos online. Push: git push. Pull: git pull. Branches for features: git branch, git checkout. Merge when ready. .gitignore lists files Git should ignore (node_modules, .env, build folders).
examples: git checkout -b new-feature — creates and switches branch

keyTerms.branch: Parallel code version for independent development
keyTerms.gitignore: File listing patterns Git should not track

quiz.question: GitHub is:
quiz.explanation: GitHub hosts repos for sharing and collaboration.

lessons.title: Deploying Your Website
lessons.content: Deployment puts your site on the internet. Static sites host free on GitHub Pages, Netlify, Vercel. GitHub Pages: push to GitHub → Settings → Pages → select branch → live at username.github.io/repo. Custom domains: buy domain, point DNS to host. Pre-deploy: check links, images, responsiveness. Optimize: compress images, minify CSS/JS, use caching. HTTPS is essential for security — most hosts provide free SSL certificates.
examples: GitHub Pages: push to main → Settings → Pages → live in minutes
Netlify: drag and drop folder → deployed with HTTPS
Custom domain: buy example.com → set DNS → site live

keyTerms.hosting: Service storing and serving your files
keyTerms.HTTPS: Secure version of HTTP — encrypts data between browser and server

quiz.question: Free static hosting:
quiz.explanation: GitHub Pages hosts static sites free.

quiz.question: Deployment means:
quiz.explanation: Making your finished site publicly accessible.

quiz.question: Before deploying, check:
quiz.explanation: Test everything before going live.

quiz.question: HTTPS is important because:
options: It encrypts data between browser and server
It only works on some browsers
quiz.explanation: HTTPS protects user data in transit — essential for security and trust.

quiz.question: To use a custom domain:

lessons.title: Web Accessibility (a11y)
lessons.content: Accessibility ensures websites are usable by everyone, including people with disabilities. WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) sets the standards. Key principles: Perceivable (alt text, captions, sufficient contrast), Operable (keyboard navigation, no time limits, skip links), Understandable (clear language, consistent navigation, error guidance), Robust (works with assistive technologies like screen readers). Practical steps: use semantic HTML, add alt text to all images, ensure color contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1, make forms label-able, ensure keyboard-only navigation works, use ARIA labels when needed. Testing: use screen readers, keyboard-only navigation, and tools like axe or Lighthouse.
examples: Alt text:
Skip link: Skip to main content — lets keyboard users bypass navigation
Color contrast: #333 text on #fff background = 12.6:1 ratio (well above 4.5:1 minimum)

keyTerms.accessibility: Making websites usable by people with all abilities and disabilities
keyTerms.WCAG: Web Content Accessibility Guidelines — the international standard for web accessibility
keyTerms.ARIA: Accessible Rich Internet Applications — attributes that enhance accessibility for dynamic content
keyTerms.screen reader: Software that reads web content aloud for visually impaired users

quiz.question: WCAG stands for:
quiz.explanation: WCAG sets the international standards for web accessibility.

quiz.question: Minimum color contrast ratio should be:
quiz.explanation: WCAG requires at least 4.5:1 contrast ratio for normal text.

quiz.question: Alt text should:
options: Describe the image's content and function
quiz.explanation: Good alt text describes what the image shows and why it matters.

quiz.question: Why is keyboard navigation important?
options: Many users can't use a mouse — motor disabilities, screen readers
quiz.explanation: Users with motor disabilities and screen reader users navigate entirely by keyboard.

quiz.question: ARIA labels are used when:
options: HTML semantics alone can't convey the meaning to assistive tech
quiz.explanation: ARIA supplements HTML semantics — use native HTML first, ARIA when needed.

lessons.title: Web Performance Optimization
lessons.content: Fast websites retain users — 53% of mobile users leave if a page takes over 3 seconds. Optimize images: compress (use WebP format), set dimensions, lazy-load below-the-fold images. Minimize HTTP requests: combine CSS/JS files, use CSS sprites for icons. Minify code: remove whitespace and comments from production CSS/JS. Enable browser caching: returning visitors load cached resources. Use CDN (Content Delivery Network): serves files from servers closest to the user. Core Web Vitals (Google's metrics): LCP (Largest Contentful Paint — main content loads fast), FID (First Input Delay — responds to clicks quickly), CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift — page doesn't jump around). Test with Google Lighthouse, PageSpeed Insights, or browser dev tools.
examples: Lazy loading: — only loads when scrolled into view
Minified CSS: body{margin:0;font-family:Arial} vs body { margin: 0; font-family: Arial; }
CDN: instead of serving images from your server in Uganda, a CDN serves them from a nearby server in Kenya

keyTerms.lazy loading: Loading images/resources only when they're about to be visible
keyTerms.minification: Removing whitespace and comments from code to reduce file size
keyTerms.CDN: Content Delivery Network — servers worldwide that serve content from the nearest location
keyTerms.Core Web Vitals: Google's metrics for measuring real-world user experience

quiz.question: Users leave if a page takes over:
quiz.explanation: 53% of mobile users abandon pages taking over 3 seconds to load.

quiz.question: Lazy loading means:
options: Loading resources only when needed (as user scrolls)
quiz.explanation: Images below the fold load only when the user scrolls near them.

quiz.question: A CDN improves speed by:
options: Serving content from servers closest to the user
quiz.explanation: CDN distributes content globally — users get it from the nearest server.

quiz.question: LCP measures:
options: How fast the main content loads
quiz.explanation: Largest Contentful Paint = time for the biggest visible element to render.

quiz.question: WebP images are preferred because:
options: Smaller file size with same quality as JPEG/PNG
quiz.explanation: WebP typically produces 25-35% smaller files than JPEG at equivalent quality.
